## 1. Pontiac Fiero goes to space — F9 (2021)
`ev-ff09-06` · ≥ 35 MU (envelope 32–41) · < 1 in 10^35 · confidence high

**Depicted.** Tej and Roman ride a rocket-powered Pontiac Fiero dropped from a carrier aircraft at 50,000 ft. They reach orbit in duct-taped, wetsuit-like suits with scuba-style helmets. When the car's magnet fails, they ram the Aries satellite and destroy it, then drift to the International Space Station, whose crew spots them and brings them back to Earth.
**Inferred.** One recap says the launch platform is a drone; three say a plane at 50,000 ft.
**Visually unverified:** re-entry is not depicted

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | The rocket bolted to a Fiero delivers about 9 km/s of delta-v | E2 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | tej (controller), roman (occupant) |
| c2 | physics | A car body with bolted fins survives supersonic ascent without tumbling or breaking up | E2 | 2 / 3 / 5 | tej (controller), roman (occupant) |
| c3 | survival | Two men survive vacuum in duct-taped wetsuits and scuba helmets | E2 | 3 / 4 / 6 | tej (survivor), roman (survivor) |
| c4 | coincidence | A hand-flown ascent intercepts one specific satellite on the first attempt | E3 | 3 / 4 / 6 | tej (controller), roman (occupant) |
| c5 | coincidence | After ramming the satellite, the unpowered car drifts to the International Space Station | E3 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | tej (beneficiary), roman (beneficiary) |

- **c1** Orbit needs 9.3-9.8 km/s from the ground; the 15 km air launch saves only a few hundred m/s. Even at a generous 300 s specific impulse the rocket equation needs a mass ratio of about 21, i.e. about 30 t of propellant for a 1.5 t vehicle. The tanks shown hold well under 1 t. The shortfall is more than 30x, a hard limit; capped. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Given c1, a car is aerodynamically unstable (centre of pressure ahead of centre of mass) and not built for the loads at maximum dynamic pressure. Real rockets need active guidance to stay pointed. Judged 1 in 100 to 1 in 100,000. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1. A separate failure mode (stability and structure, not propellant).
- **c3** Above the Armstrong limit (19 km) a suit must hold a stable internal pressure over the whole body. A wetsuit is not a pressure garment; one leak means ebullism and unconsciousness in seconds. Both suits must hold for the whole flight. Judged 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000,000. *Dependence:* Conditional on c2; one component for both men (same improvised design).
- **c4** Orbital rendezvous needs matched plane, altitude, phase and velocity. Gemini-era crews did it with onboard computers and ground tracking; a single launch window with manual control is judged 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000,000. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1-c3.
- **c5** Reaching the ISS needs the same orbital plane (a plane change costs km/s) and a near match in altitude, phase and velocity. The chance that an arbitrary orbit after a collision passes within reach of the ISS with a matched velocity is far below one in a trillion (the orbital shell alone is ~2e10 km3). Capped. *Dependence:* Conditional on c4. Separate from c4 because the satellite's orbit is not the ISS's orbit.

## 2. The endless runway — Fast & Furious 6 (2013)
`ev-ff06-04` · ≥ 24 MU (envelope 24–24) · < 1 in 10^24 · confidence high

**Depicted.** The team chases Shaw's accelerating Antonov cargo plane down the runway for roughly 13 minutes and anchors it with cables from their cars to stop it taking off.
**Inferred.** Several independent analyses (including the screenwriter's own) put the implied runway at 26-29 miles. The Fandom account places Dom, Letty, Brian and Hobbs aboard the plane while Han, Gisele, Roman, Tej, Brian and Mia tether it from their cars; the tether component is credited to the latter group.

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | Cars tethered by cables hold down a heavy cargo plane at takeoff power | E2 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | han (controller), gisele (controller), roman (controller), tej (controller), brian (controller), mia (controller) |
| c2 | coincidence | The runway keeps going for 26-29 miles | E1 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | dom (beneficiary), brian (beneficiary), roman (beneficiary), tej (beneficiary), han (beneficiary), gisele (beneficiary), letty (beneficiary), mia (beneficiary), hobbs (beneficiary), owen (beneficiary) |

- **c1** An An-124 makes about 900 kN of thrust and, near rotation speed, about 4 MN of lift. A car's braking or anchoring force is about 16 kN (0.9 x 1.8 t x g). Even several cars supply under 100 kN, one-ninth of the thrust and a small fraction of the lift. This is a hard-limit violation, capped at the Record Horizon. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Given c1 (the plane is held down at speed), the chase needs 26-29 miles of runway. No runway on Earth exceeds about 3.4 miles, so the frequency of such a runway is zero among all observed airfields; capped at the Record Horizon. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1. Without c1 the plane lifts off within about 3 km and no long runway is needed, so the two failure modes are separate.

## 3. Two Chargers drag a bank vault through Rio — Fast Five (2011)
`ev-ff05-03` · ≥ 16 MU (envelope 14.5–19) · < 1 in 10^16 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** Dom and Brian chain two 2010 Dodge Chargers to Reyes's evidence vault, tear it out of the police station and drag it at speed through the city, swinging it into pursuing cars and buildings.
**Inferred.** The vault's mass is not stated; an 8 ft steel vault weighs roughly 20-40 t.

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | Two Chargers generate enough pulling force to drag a 20-40 t steel vault | E2 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | dom (controller), brian (controller) |
| c2 | physics | The cars stay controllable while a mass 10-20x heavier swings on 30 ft cables through corners | E2 | 2 / 3 / 5 | dom (controller), brian (controller) |
| c3 | skill | Dom aims the swinging vault into specific targets | E4 | 0.5 / 1 / 2 | dom (performer) |

- **c1** Sliding steel on asphalt needs at least 0.3 x m x g: 59 kN for a 20 t vault. Two Chargers can push at most about 17 kN before their tyres spin. The requirement exceeds tyre grip by 3-7x, so this is a hard-limit violation, capped at the Record Horizon. The production confirms the limit: it cut a shot of the vault hanging off the bridge because "even the powerful Chargers would not be able to support the vault's weight". *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Granting c1, a swinging 20 t mass exerts lateral cable loads far above each car's lateral grip (about 17 kN). Every wide swing should drag both cars sideways. Staying on course through a city chase needs the swing to stay small at every corner; judged 1 in 100 to 1 in 100,000. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1. This is a separate failure mode (lateral control, not forward traction).
- **c3** A pendulum on a cable steered by one of two independently driven cars. Judgment prior around 1 in 10 per aimed hit. *Dependence:* Conditional on c2 (the cars are controllable at all).

## 4. Hobbs holds a Black Hawk by its chain — Hobbs & Shaw (2019)
`ev-hs-05` · ≥ 13 MU (envelope 12.5–14) · < 1 in 10^13 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** The Hobbs family chains a convoy of trucks to Brixton's UH-60 Black Hawk in a cliffside tug-of-war. When the chain breaks, Hobbs grabs it and holds the helicopter back with his own strength.
**Inferred.** The chain was CGI and the cliffside road is a constructed, composited set. The helicopter and the trucks were largely practical (the director says about 95%).
**Visually unverified:** whether Hobbs is braced or anchored

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | A chained convoy of trucks holds a Black Hawk and the pilot keeps control with a tether attached | E2 | 0.5 / 1 / 2 | hobbs (controller), deckard (controller) |
| c2 | physics | One man holds a helicopter that is pulling with 20-40 kN | E2 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | hobbs (controller) |

- **c1** This part is roughly plausible. The Black Hawk's excess lift is about 20-40 kN, and a 9 t truck resists about 90 kN. The real risk is dynamic rollover from a side-pulling tether, which pilots train to avoid. Judged about 1 in 10. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** The heaviest deadlift ever is 510 kg, about 5 kN, lifted with legs, a bar and ideal footing. The helicopter's excess lift is 4-8x that, and friction under Hobbs's feet is only about 1 kN. Hard limit; capped. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1 (the helicopter is tethered and flyable when the chain breaks).

## 5. Brixton runs down a skyscraper's slanted face carrying Hattie — Hobbs & Shaw (2019)
`ev-hs-02` · ≥ 12 MU (envelope 12–12) · < 1 in 10^12 · confidence low

**Depicted.** Brixton grabs Hattie, exits a high window, and runs down the steeply slanted exterior face of the tower to street level.
**Inferred.** The filming reference is the 225 m Leadenhall Building, whose one face slants like a wedge.
**In-universe excuse (ignored for scoring).** Cybernetically rebuilt legs and grip.
**Visually unverified:** slope angle of the face; height descended

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | A runner controls his speed down a glass face far steeper than 45 degrees | E2 | 12 / 12 / 12 (cap, lower bound) | brixton (controller), hattie (occupant) |

- **c1** To descend without accelerating, friction must exceed tan(slope): 1.0 at 45 degrees and 5.7 at 80 degrees. Shoe rubber on glass gives about 0.5-1.0. Stronger legs do not change friction, so on any face steep enough to look like a skyscraper he is sliding at close to free fall. Hard limit; capped. Low confidence because the on-screen angle is not measured. *Dependence:* First component.

## 6. Charger swings across the gorge on the bridge's rope — F9 (2021)
`ev-ff09-02` · 7.5 MU (envelope 4.5–12.5) · 1 in 3×10^7 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** With the rope bridge collapsed, Dom drives his Charger off the cliff toward its remains, snags a rope from the bridge, swings across on it and lands on the far cliffside.
**Inferred.** The bridge had just carried Tej's Jeep before collapsing. The Fandom sequence page puts Letty in Dom's Charger for this jump, after she is thrown from her motorcycle in the minefield.
**Visually unverified:** gap width

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | coincidence | A car driven off a cliff snags a dangling rope so that it is securely attached | E4 | 1 / 1.5 / 2.5 | dom (controller), letty (occupant) |
| c2 | physics | A single old bridge rope holds a 2 t car at the bottom of the swing | E2 | 3 / 5 / 8 | dom (controller), letty (occupant) |
| c3 | coincidence | The swing releases the car onto the far cliff rather than into its face | E3 | 0.5 / 1 / 2 | dom (controller), letty (occupant) |

- **c1** The rope must catch on a part of the car that holds (not slide off the bodywork). Judgment prior about 1 in 30. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Tension at the bottom of the swing is m(g + v2/L): with v = 20-30 m/s and L = 30 m that is 2 t x 23-40 m/s2 = 46-80 kN, before the shock load of the catch. A weathered natural-fibre rope of this size breaks at roughly 10-40 kN. The requirement is 2-8x the rope's strength. Judged 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100 million. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1.
- **c3** A pendulum returns to its release height only at the same side unless the pivot and timing work out. Judged about 1 in 10. *Dependence:* Conditional on c2.

## 7. Hobbs redirects a torpedo by hand — The Fate of the Furious (2017)
`ev-ff08-04` · 7 MU (envelope 3.5–14) · 1 in 10^7 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** Leaning out of his vehicle at speed on the frozen lake, Hobbs grabs a live torpedo skidding across the ice and shoves it into another vehicle.
**Visually unverified:** deflection angle; whether Hobbs's vehicle matches the torpedo's speed; whether this is the same on-screen beat as ev-ff08-06 (sources say torpedo and missile; unresolved)

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | One arm, from a moving vehicle, turns a 2 t torpedo moving at about 50 mph | E2 | 3 / 6 / 12 | hobbs (controller) |
| c2 | coincidence | Grabbing the torpedo does not set it off, but hitting the target vehicle does | E4 | 0.5 / 1 / 2 | hobbs (beneficiary) |

- **c1** Lateral impulse F = m x v x sin(theta) / t, with m = 2 t and v = 22 m/s. The four corners of 3-10 degrees over 0.5-1 s give 2.3 kN, 4.6 kN, 7.6 kN and 15.3 kN. The heaviest deadlift ever is about 5 kN with both legs and ideal footing; a one-arm pull while leaning from a moving vehicle is perhaps 1-1.5 kN. The requirement is therefore 1.5x to 15x the plausible force: marginal at the gentlest corner, far beyond it at the sharpest. It is not capped because the gentlest corner, which is the assumption most favourable to the stunt, stays under 3x. The wide MU range is deliberate. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Contact fuzes are built to fire on impacts far softer than a car collision; the ice skid, the grab and the hit form a narrow sequence. Judgment prior about 1 in 10. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1.

Sources: [Stunts Unlimited: F8 stunt reveal (ice, torpedo grab, car blasts)](https://stuntsunlimited.com/f8_stunt_reveal/), [TheWrap: Fate of the Furious fact check (torpedo redirect)](https://www.thewrap.com/fate-of-the-furious-fact-check-could-those-crazy-stunts-really-happen/)

## 8. Five cars parachuted onto a mountain road — Furious 7 (2015)
`ev-ff07-01` · 6 MU (envelope 4–8.5) · 1 in 10^6 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** The crew, sitting in their cars, are dropped from a C-130 over the Caucasus, parachute down, land on the mountain road and immediately drive into the attack on Jakande's convoy.
**Inferred.** Each named driver has a car (five cars); the production dropped four real cars from 12,000 ft.
**Visually unverified:** whether every car lands on the road surface itself

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | coincidence | All five cars land on (not merely near) a narrow mountain road | E3 | 3 / 4.5 / 6 | dom (controller), brian (controller), letty (controller), roman (controller), tej (controller) |
| c2 | physics | Each car lands on its tyres under a cargo parachute and drives off at once | E4 | 1 / 1.5 / 2.5 | dom (occupant), brian (occupant), letty (occupant), roman (occupant), tej (occupant) |

- **c1** The best fielded guided airdrop system lands within 50-75 m. With about 50 m of error across the road, the chance of landing within +/-4 m of the road's centre line is about 6% per car (1.2 MU). Five cars would give 6 MU if independent; wind errors are shared, so the central estimate credits partial correlation. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Cargo parachutes land at 7-9 m/s, like dropping a car from 3-4 m. Military airdrops land vehicles on crushable honeycomb platforms precisely because tyres and suspension fail. The production's own landing shots used cars on wires dropped 6-10 ft onto moving wheels. Judged 1 in 3 per car, correlated. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1 (the car is over the road).

Sources: [Wikipedia: Furious 7, plot and production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furious_7), [Fast & Furious Wiki: Furious 7 plot](https://fastandfurious.fandom.com/wiki/Furious_7), [Screen Rant: how the Furious 7 cargo-plane car drop was filmed](https://screenrant.com/fast-furious-7-cargo-plane-cars-stunt-filmed/)

**Depicted.** Letty is thrown from the overturning tank off the elevated highway. Dom drives off the edge, intercepts her in mid-air on his windshield, and the car lands on a parked vehicle below. Both survive and walk away.
**Inferred.** The highway's height is a VFX exaggeration of a lower real road.
**Visually unverified:** drop height; relative speed at the catch

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **c1** Two projectiles must meet within about 1 m in each of three dimensions. Dom commits before Letty's trajectory is known; a timing error of +/-0.3 s at ~25 m/s is +/-7 m, against a catch zone of ~1 m, and launch angle adds a similar error vertically. Joint success is roughly 1 in 100 to 1 in 10,000. *Dependence:* First component.
- **c2** Dan's Reality Check puts the catch impact alone as lethal at the implied 60 mph. Even at a lower relative speed, Letty is unrestrained on the car's exterior when it lands on another vehicle. ## 11. Driving down the face of a 460 ft dam — Fast X (2023)
`ev-ff10-03` · 4.5 MU (envelope 3–7) · 1 in 30,000 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** Boxed in between two drone-driven tanker trucks on top of a dam, Dom drives off the edge with his son Little B, down the dam's face, and lands in the water below. Both are shown alive before Dante blows up the dam.
**Inferred.** The real Aldeadávila Dam is 460 ft; the director described it as a "vertical quarter mile".
**Visually unverified:** slope of the face as depicted

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | skill | The car stays wheels-down on a near-vertical 140 m face instead of tumbling | E4 | 0.5 / 1 / 2 | dom (performer) |
| c2 | survival | Father and child survive a 140 m descent ending in water at about 50 m/s, and are functional | E1 | 2.5 / 3.5 / 5 | dom (survivor), little_b (survivor) |

- **c1** On a near-vertical face the tyres barely load, so steering is almost useless; judged about 1 in 10. *Dependence:* First component.

Golden Gate data: a 75 m fall into water is survived about 2% of the time, with major injuries. A 140 m descent is worse (about 0.1-0.5% survival), and both are shown alive and alert. The car's frame and belts help somewhat. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1; one component for both occupants.

## 12. Outrunning landmines at 80 mph — F9 (2021)
`ev-ff09-01` · 4 MU (envelope 2.5–7) · 1 in 10,000 · confidence medium

**Depicted.** Fleeing soldiers, the team drives into a minefield. Tej tells everyone to stay above 80 mph "to avoid being blown up"; they race through as mines detonate around them. Roman's car is destroyed and he barely escapes the blast.
**Visually unverified:** whether mines detonate behind or under the cars

| # | Category | Claim | Evidence | MU low / central / high | Credited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | physics | Driving fast enough to be clear of a pressure-triggered mine before it explodes | E2 | 2 / 3 / 5 | dom (controller), letty (controller), roman (controller), tej (controller), ramsey (occupant) |
| c2 | survival | Roman escapes a mine blast that destroys his car | E4 | 0.5 / 1 / 2 | roman (survivor) |

- **c1** Anti-vehicle mines fire within milliseconds of pressure; at 80 mph (36 m/s) a car moves about 4 cm per millisecond. Getting about 5 m clear needs a fuze delay of about 140 ms, which standard pressure fuzes do not have. Speed only helps if every mine in the field has an unusual delay. Judged 1 in 100 to 1 in 100,000. *Dependence:* First component; one component for all cars (the mines are the same type).
- **c2** Anti-vehicle mines are designed to kill a vehicle's occupants. Judgment prior about 1 in 10. *Dependence:* Conditional on c1 failing locally for Roman's car (the mine catches his car but not him).
